a: Several highly influential art movements are rarely discussed today despite their profound impact on the development of art. The Artesian movement, also known as the Hague School, emerged in the Netherlands in the 1860s and 1870s, focusing on realistic depictions of rural life and landscapes. Its emphasis on natural light and everyday subjects influenced the development of Impressionism. The Ukiyo-e movement in Japan, which flourished from the 17th to 19th centuries, produced woodblock prints that profoundly influenced Western artists like Van Gogh, Monet, and Debussy, contributing to the Japonisme craze. The Bengal School of Art, active in the early 20th century, sought to revive traditional Indian artistic techniques while incorporating modern elements, influencing artists across Asia. The Mexican Muralism movement of the 1920s and 1930s, led by Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco, and David Alfaro Siqueiros, used large-scale public murals to communicate social and political messages, influencing public art worldwide. The Bauhaus movement, though well-known among design professionals, is rarely discussed in popular culture despite revolutionizing architecture, typography, and industrial design. The De Stijl movement, founded in the Netherlands in 1917, developed a vocabulary of geometric abstraction and neoplasticism that influenced modern architecture and design. The Synchromism movement, founded by Stanton MacDonald-Wright and Morgan Russell in 1913, was one of the first American avant-garde movements to gain international recognition, predating Abstract Expressionism. The Precisionist movement in America, active in the 1920s and 1930s, celebrated the machine age through clean, geometric depictions of industrial landscapes and factories. The Socialist Realism movement, though politically controversial, was highly influential in shaping public art and propaganda across multiple countries. The Négritude movement, founded by Aimé Césaire and Léopold Sédar Senghor in the 1930s, used art and literature to assert African cultural identity and resist colonialism, influencing the Harlem Renaissance and post-colonial art movements. The Gutai group, founded in Japan in 1954, was one of the first post-war avant-garde movements to explore performance and conceptual art, influencing Fluxus and Happenings. These movements, while less familiar to the general public, have had a lasting impact on the trajectory of art history and continue to influence contemporary artistic practice.
